qt: to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

The UK Government has admitted that carbon emissions from data centres could be 100 times greater than previously thought. Revised analysis accompanying a government ‘Compute Roadmap’ shows that UK greenhouse gas emissions from artificial intelligence (AI) could reach 123 million metric tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2), the equivalent of 3.4 percent of the UK’s emissions, between 2025 and 2035. That is significantly higher than a forecast published in July 2025 of up to 0.142 MtCO2 from AI in 2035. The initial modelling was withdrawn in March in order to ‘reflect new analysis’. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission wish to also update its reply to my parliamentary question E004535/20251?
Does the Commission expect that it will be possible for the EU to remain competitive in the AI sector while maintaining all the EU’s emissions targets?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.10.2026) As stated in its reply to Question E-004535/20251, the Commission is aware of the impacts of AI and stays committed to addressing them to reach its 2050 climate neutrality objective. It will continue to assess future developments considering the available evidence. In the last six months, the available evidence has not changed the previous estimations. Digital growth and high sustainability standards can mutually reinforce each other. If well integrated in the energy system, AI can contribute to reducing emissions and energy system costs, by optimising energy system efficiency, integration and flexibility, and data centres can actively contribute to the clean energy transition by supporting, among others, renewable energy deployment and waste heat recovery. To start tackling the challenges the expansion of data centres entails for the energy system, the EU has already introduced a reporting scheme2 to collect and assess the energy and sustainability performance of data centres. In addition, the Commission has recently proposed a Union rating scheme, a label3, and has launched a public consultation on minimum performance standards4. These initiatives are closely interrelated with the proposal for a Cloud and AI Development Act5, which promotes the deployment of data centres adhering to high environmental and energy efficiency standards by mandating Member States to include such standards in their national cloud and AI strategies and incentivizes the data centre sector to transition to a clean energy system including through onsite generation and storage of clean energy. These initiatives aim to ensure that growth in AI and cloud services is not only possible, but sustainable.
